methods.name: DrawTerminatorOn
methods.description: THE NIGHT SIDE, drawn. The terminator is a great circle, so on most projections it is a curve that leaves the sheet at one edge and comes back at the other -- which is why it is drawn as a LINE over a shading rather than as a filled polygon: a polygon would have to decide what "inside" means on a projection that cuts it, and would get it wrong at exactly the two solstices.
methods.signature: DrawTerminatorOn(poCanvas, pnYear, pnMonth, pnDay, pnHourUtc, pInk, pnWidth)

methods.name: DrawNightOn
methods.description: FOUR NESTED CAPS give the gradient a reader sees at dusk: the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon at 84 from the antipode, nautical at 78, astronomical at 72. Drawn outermost first, each translucent, so they ACCUMULATE -- the deepest night is four layers deep and full dark is reached gradually rather than in one step.
methods.signature: DrawNightOn(poCanvas, pnYear, pnMonth, pnDay, pnHourUtc, pInk)

methods.name: DrawTwilightOn
methods.description: ...and the twilight bands with it, each fainter than the last, which is what a day-night map actually looks like
methods.signature: DrawTwilightOn(poCanvas, pnYear, pnMonth, pnDay, pnHourUtc, pInk)

methods.name: DrawVectorsRampedOn
methods.description: An arrow's LENGTH is the natural encoding and it is a poor one at small sizes: a reader compares two short strokes by eye and gets the ordering, not the ratio. Colour gives the ratio. Wolfram's VectorPlot uses both together and that is why its fields read at a glance, so this does too -- and the two agreeing is what makes a long arrow read as fast rather than merely as long.
methods.signature: DrawVectorsRampedOn(poCanvas, paGrid, paU, paV, pnEvery, pnPxPerUnit, pcRamp, pnWidth)

methods.signature: DrawVectorsOn(poCanvas, paGrid, paU, paV, pnEvery, pnPxPerUnit, pInk, pnWidth)

methods.name: DrawStreamlinesOn
methods.description: Euler's method is three lines shorter and spirals OUTWARD on a field that rotates -- so a closed circular flow comes back as an opening spiral, which a reader takes for a real divergence rather than for the integrator's own error. RK4 costs four samples a step and holds the circle to a part in ten thousand over three thousand steps.
methods.signature: DrawStreamlinesOn(poCanvas, paGrid, paU, paV, paSeeds, pnStepDeg, pnSteps, pInk, pnWidth)

methods.name: DrawFlowOn
methods.description: The stroke then varies with SPEED, because a streamline of constant width says every part of the flow is equally fast, and that is the one thing a streamline cannot otherwise deny.
methods.signature: DrawFlowOn(poCanvas, paGrid, paU, paV, pnSepDeg, pInk)

methods.name: DrawFlowRampedOn
methods.description: Colour is the strongest channel there is for a scalar. Width is one of the weakest, and it is spent here anyway -- kept as a SECOND encoding of the same quantity, because the two agreeing is what makes a fast line read as fast rather than merely as orange.
methods.signature: DrawFlowRampedOn(poCanvas, paGrid, paU, paV, pnSepDeg, pcRamp, pHeadInk)

methods.name: SpeedField
methods.description: THE LINES ARE ONE DARK INK, not the ramp. The colour is in the ground now, and a second colour scale on the lines would be two encodings of one quantity fighting for the same eye. The flow's job over a density is to show the SHAPE; the ground shows the magnitude. THE SPEED AT EVERY NODE, sqrt(u^2 + v^2) -- the scalar a stream-density plot shades, exposed so a caller can hand it to a stzGeoField of their own, and so the property that the background IS the magnitude can be checked rather than trusted.

methods.name: ClarkEvans
methods.description: EDGE-CORRECTED, BY DONNELLY. Uncorrected, the index leans toward "dispersed" on every real window -- a point near the border has no neighbours beyond it -- and five hundred uniform points in a window the shape of a country read as dispersed at z = 2.0 the first time this ran. The correction uses the window's perimeter, which is why a pattern carries its window. ClarkEvansUncorrected() is the naive one, for comparison and for readers who know the older literature.

methods.name: RipleyK
methods.description: Ripley's K at each radius, UNCORRECTED FOR THE EDGE. Points near the window's border have fewer neighbours within r than they would in an infinite plane, so K falls short at large r. This is not corrected by formula; it is answered by Envelope(), which simulates the null under the same edge.

methods.name: HasInteraction
methods.description: DOES THIS PROCESS PLACE POINTS WITHOUT REGARD TO ONE ANOTHER? The three that do are the honest null models -- whatever a statistic sees in their output is chance. The four that do not have an interaction built in, and are what a caller tests FOR.

methods.name: SetIntensity
methods.description: the parameters, under the names they have in the subject ------------- points per square kilometre -- :Poisson, :MaternII

methods.name: SetCount
methods.description: how many points exactly -- :Binomial, :SSI

methods.name: SetParentIntensity
methods.description: clusters per square kilometre -- :MaternCluster, :Thomas. The parents are NEVER DRAWN: they are where the clusters are, not points of the pattern, and a reader who saw them would be looking at a mechanism rather than at data.

methods.name: SetRadiusKm
methods.description: the radius of a Matern cluster's disc, km

methods.name: SetSigmaKm
methods.description: the scale of a Thomas cluster's Gaussian, km. It is NOT a radius: about a third of the children land beyond it and a few land far out, which is the whole difference from Matern and is a claim about the mechanism.

methods.name: SetHardCoreKm
methods.description: the distance no two points may come within -- :MaternII, :SSI

methods.name: SetIntensityField
methods.description: THE INTENSITY SURFACE of an inhomogeneous process, as a GE7b field. That is not a workaround for the engine taking no callbacks: a kernel density estimated from one pattern IS such a field, so the natural workflow -- read a population surface, then ask whether the cases are clustered beyond it -- is two calls with nothing in between.

methods.name: ExpectedCount
methods.description: For the two CLUSTER processes this is the count BEFORE the window clips it. Children thrown outside are lost, and how many depends on how far the mechanism scatters them -- measured on a one-degree square, a Matern cluster of radius 8 km loses 6 per cent and a Thomas of sigma 4 km loses 17, because a Gaussian has no edge. The loss is real and it is the window's, not the process's.

methods.name: GenerateIn
methods.description: ONE PATTERN FROM THIS PROCESS, inside a window, as a flat lon/lat list.

methods.name: PatternIn
methods.description: ...and the same as a stzGeoPoints, ready to be measured

methods.name: EnvelopeOf
methods.description: THIRTY-NINE IS THE CLASSIC COUNT, and it is not a floor to be raised for free precision: the band WIDENS with the number of simulations, so an envelope of 999 is a stricter test than an envelope of 39 and the two are not comparable. Being the most extreme of forty is a one-in-forty event under the null -- 2.5 per cent on each side. The count belongs in whatever gets reported.

methods.name: EscapesOf
methods.description: WHERE AN OBSERVED PATTERN ESCAPES THIS PROCESS'S BAND, and which way: -1 below, 0 inside, +1 above. A reader wants the RANGE OF SCALES at which a pattern is unusual, not one verdict -- a wood can be clustered at ten metres and regular at fifty, and a single p-value cannot say that.

methods.name: VerdictOn
methods.description: THE VERDICT IN WORDS, with the scales it holds at -- which is the only honest summary, because "clustered" without a range is not a finding.

methods.description: THE REGISTRATION GATE (ruling 3.2a) ------------------------------------ May this actor EXIST in a loop at all -- asked before any tick, when the answer is still free. MayProceed gates ACTS; this gates REGISTRATION, and those are different failures. One rule, two doors, same words: the sentences are agentloop.zig's own refusals (AGENTLOOP-R4 / AGENTLOOP-R5), quoted with only the engine's slot number absent, so a caller who meets the refusal in either door reads the same law.

methods.name: UploadQ
methods.description: Upload a vector; it lives on the device until Free() (or eviction under VRAM pressure -- bounded, counted, never silent).

methods.name: Run
methods.description: One-shot convenience: upload the bound vectors, run the kernel, read the result back, free everything temporary. Data in, DATA out.

methods.name: ApplyOnQ

methods.name: Calibrate
methods.description: Measure where the GPU actually starts winning ON THIS MACHINE, store the crossover in the calibration store, and persist it (the faces auto-load it in later sessions). Warm-min discipline throughout -- G0's clock inversion means sustained numbers flatter the GPU. Returns [ nThreshold, [ [nProblemSize, nCpuMs, nGpuMs], ... ] ].

methods.name: CalibrateWith
methods.description: The same, on a caller-chosen ladder of corpus sizes (d fixed at 64: a representative embedding width; problem size = n*d).

methods.name: Verify
methods.description: pCand may be an stzKernelMaker on the SAME declarations, or raw WGSL on the same binding contract (how a hand-written variant -- or a cheat -- gets checked). Options: [ :reps = 7, :band = 0.000001 ].

methods.name: VerifyJudge
methods.description: The roofline alone: could a dispatch touching nBytes finish in nMs on this device? Pure judgement over the MEASURED floors -- exposed so a guard can hand it an impossible number and watch it refuse.

methods.name: VerifyFloors
methods.description: The measured floors themselves: [ :floorgbs, :submitfloorms ]

methods.name: FirstError
methods.description: one rung: warm-min per-query ms through the REAL seam, both routes Measured 2026-09-09 on this laptop's RTX 3050: after ~10 s idle, every submit pays a fixed ~2 ms and the copy floor reads 13 GB/s instead of 85 -- and hundreds of tiny queries never lift it, while ~150 ms of heavy work does. Wake() is that work, ADAPTIVE: it copies until a copy runs at full speed, settles, and stops -- the budget is a cap. Every timing this face takes calls it first; a caller measuring on its own should too. Returns the copies it took (an awake device answers in ~20). THE CAUSE AND THE SYMPTOM. A shader that fails validation raises two errors: the parser's, with the offending name and line, and then the pipeline's, which only says the module is invalid. FirstError() is the parser's; LastError() is whatever came last. A compile clears both first.

methods.name: CalibrateKnnResident
methods.description: Measured 2026-09-09 on the RTX 3050 laptop at 384 dims: the GPU loses at 1,000 (0.39x) and 4,000 (0.98x) and wins at 16,000 (1.42x); the multicore top-k switches on at n*d >= 8M and the window may close again above it -- which is why the rung above that gate is measured too, and why the store is SHAPED: a class that wins carries its win, and the flat line stays beyond the ladder where a class lost.

methods.name: ConvolveReal
methods.description: This is the ONE-SHOT doorway: upload, run, download. A plane holding its signal on the device uses the buffer form (StzEngineGpuOpConvolveReal over buffer ids) and pays no marshalling -- the sound desk's route.

methods.name: FoundryPairdist
methods.description: Report: [ :m, :n, :d, :hiddenn, :clocks, :refgpums, :refwallms, :variants = [ [name, verified, gpums, wallms, ratio, ratiowall], ... ], :winner = name, :ratio = generic/winner on the GPU clock, :stored = bool ]

methods.name: FoundryAttention
methods.description: THE ATTENTION FOUNDRY (GK2c). The backbone's fused attention -- one workgroup per (head, query row) -- against three reduction-form variants at workgroup widths 64, 128 and 256, under the checker on the neural DLL's device; the winner recorded for the (tokens, width, head_dim) class under the op name "attention", persisted, and pushed into the neural DLL's table so the next forward dispatches it.

methods.name: FoundryMatmul
methods.description: THE MATMUL FOUNDRY (GK2b's matmul leg). C(m x n) = A(m x k) B(k x n): tile16 (the generic), tile8, reg2, reg4 under the checker at the asked shape and a hidden one; the winner recorded for the (m, n, k) class under the op name "matmul" and persisted. The backbone compiles the table's winner for its own shapes with the bias fused.

methods.name: FoundryUmapKnn
methods.description: THE k-NN FOUNDRY (GS6e). The UMAP k-NN kernel lives in the stats DLL on its own device, so its enumeration runs there; the verdict is recorded in that DLL's variant table AND persisted here under the op name "umap_knn", beside pairdist's rows, so the next session finds it. The stats DLL reads the persisted rows back through StzUmapKnnVariantsSync() at its first fit.

methods.name: FoundryPairdistGrid
methods.description: The kill line, per adapter: a grid of single-query shapes; TRUE if any class found a variant worth the margin.

methods.name: CalibrateShaped

Both older spellings are kept as alternative forms, since stzOrgChart and stzWorkflow call View() internally. -- A VALUE THAT SAYS WHAT IT IS (DN9g) --------------------------------- A GRAPH HANDS OVER ITS NODES AND EDGES AND LETS THE CONSUMER LAY THEM OUT, which is exactly what the display contract's first consumer asked a graph to do. Note that Display(), just below, does something else entirely: it opens an external viewer and returns nothing.

methods.name: When
methods.description: a node-matching clause: property `pcProp` `pcOp` `pValue`. Clauses AND.

methods.name: Then
methods.description: a REQUIREMENT clause: on a node in scope (matching every When), this must hold, else the node is a finding. Turns the rule from a prohibition ("no node should match") into an implication ("every matching node must satisfy this"). Same operator set as When, incl. the comparisons.

methods.name: Governs
methods.description: supply an explicit checker for rules too rich for the clause DSL. It is called as call fChecker(oGraph) and returns [ [ :where, :message ], ... ]. WHICH SUBJECTS THIS RULE GOVERNS -- declared beside the checker, not instead of it. See the block at @fGoverns for why both are needed.

methods.name: Excludes
methods.description: ...AND WHICH IT MUST NOT. The negative sibling, at rule level: a boundary that is never exercised is a boundary that could be anywhere.

methods.name: DeclareUniversal
methods.description: A rule with no boundary because the claim genuinely has none. The reason is required: "universal" without one is indistinguishable from a scope predicate that broke, which is the case worth catching.

methods.name: SetReadsQ
methods.description: What it reads, what it writes, and when it runs -- so an ordering defect is a fact about declarations rather than something found by rendering the world and squinting at it.

methods.name: SubjectsIn
methods.description: A rule with BOTH is answered by the closure, because a closure is reached for exactly when the clauses cannot say the thing.

methods.name: CounterSubjectsIn
methods.description: ...and the boundary of a clause rule is the complement: the nodes it looked at and did not take. Free, exact, and available for every clause rule in the library without anyone writing a line.

methods.description: TEST / OFFLINE DOOR, named for what it is. It spends budget like a real call, and Why() says "FAKE responder" on every answer it produces, so nothing it returns can be mistaken for a live one. methods.name: IsAList
methods.description: So a stzList answered "no" to being a list, and every `but IsAList()` arm in the library fell past it. stzObject.IsEither() has such an arm, followed by `but IsAnObject()` -- which a stzList IS -- so comparing two lists raised "Feature not implemented yet!" from a branch meant for something else entirely.

example.from: composed from the signature, run in the library

methods.name: HasSameTypeAs
methods.description: SAME SHAPE, SAME OMISSION. stzObject.HasSameTypeAs(p) answers isObject(p), and each wrapper overrides it to test the type it WRAPS -- stzNumber asks isNumber, stzString asks isString. stzList never asked isList, so comparing a stzList to a plain list said "different type", and IsStrictlyEqualTo() -- the conjunction of same type, same content and same order -- could never be true for the one comparison it exists to make.

example.code:
o1 = new stzList([ "a", "b", "c" ])
? o1.IsStrictlyEqualTo([ "a", "b", "c" ])
? o1.HasSameTypeAs([ "a", "b", "c" ])
? o1.HasSameContentAs([ "a", "b", "c" ])
? o1.HasSameSortingOrderAs([ "a", "b", "c" ])

methods.name: Content
methods.description: Returned straight from the field. It used to be assigned to a local first, which bought nothing -- Haro copies a list on return either way, so callers were always safe -- and cost a SECOND full copy of the list on every call. Over a million numbers that was 0.32s per call, more than the whole engine crossing it was sitting in front of.

methods.name: ToStzNumBuffer
methods.description: Measured over a million numbers, eight reductions: 0.28s the ordinary way (eight marshals), 0.04s across this door (one). The boundary is NAMED at the call site rather than guessed at underneath -- the tier you are in should be something you can see. @aContent directly, NOT This.Content(): that method assigns the field to a local before returning it, so asking it costs two full copies of the list before the buffer has marshalled anything. Over a million numbers those copies cost more than the crossing they were meant to save, and the door measured SLOWER than the ordinary path until they were removed.

methods.name: MostSimilarByMeaning
methods.description: These are what make a list of TEXTS more than a list of strings. They read the MEANING of each fragment (semantic similarity, sentiment), so a fluent chain like Q(text).SentencesQ().MostSimilarByMeaning(query) / .ThatAre( :Positive) works. Semantic ops upgrade to neural embeddings when a model is loaded (StzNeuralModelQ(path)), else degrade to lexical -- see StzSemanticSimilarity(). The text most similar to pcQuery by MEANING. Uses the loaded neural model's sentence embeddings when one is present, else lexical WORD-OVERLAP cosine -- the right notion for sentences/documents. (The inherited MostSimilarTo() uses Jaro-Winkler CHARACTER similarity, better for fuzzy word/typo matching.)

methods.name: RankedForQuery

The accurate second stage of retrieve-then-rerank. RankedForQuery(query) -- [[doc, score], ...] sorted by descending relevance.

methods.name: TrainingSetQ
methods.description: THE HELD SET IS LIVE THROUGH HERE. Haro COPIES an object into an attribute, so the set handed to the constructor is a SNAPSHOT: growing the caller's own object afterwards would NOT reach this learner. Grow it through this accessor -- oLearner.TrainingSetQ().AddExample(...) -- which reaches the real held set (accessor + method call is live in Haro).

methods.name: Train
methods.description: The drift against the old loop was measured, not assumed, and it is never zero: 1e-16 after ONE epoch, 1e-15 at ten, 1e-14 at a hundred and still 1e-14 at five hundred. That is the one thing that could not be held fixed -- Haro's exp is the C library's, the engine's is Zig's, they agree to within an ulp, and gradient descent feeds each step into the next so the difference grows about a decade per five hundred epochs. Against weights of magnitude 1 to 10 it stays around 1e-15 relative, and both loops classify identically.

methods.name: Probability
methods.description: SCORED BY THE RULE IT WAS FITTED BY. This goes through the engine too, and not for speed -- one row is dominated by marshalling. It is here because Haro's exp and Zig's exp agree only to within an ulp, and a model whose predictions come from a slightly different function than its fit is a question nobody should have to think about. One definition, both ends.

methods.name: Probabilities
methods.description: Probabilities for many rows in ONE crossing. TrainingAccuracy() below is the reason this exists: it scores every training example, and a round trip per row would have made the diagnostic cost more than the fit it diagnoses.

example.code:
oDS = new stzTrainingSet([])
oDS.AddExample([ 1, 1 ], "yes")
oDS.AddExample([ 1, 0 ], "yes")
oDS.AddExample([ 0, 1 ], "no")
oDS.AddExample([ 0, 0 ], "no")
o1 = new stzLogisticRegression(oDS)
? o1.Bias()

methods.name: TrainingAccuracy
methods.description: Needing standardised features is the normal requirement for stochastic gradient descent, not a defect here -- but nothing surfaced the failure. This does: a diverged model scores around chance on data it has already seen, where a converged one scores near 1.

example.code:
oDS = new stzTrainingSet([])
oDS.AddExample([ 1, 1 ], "yes")
oDS.AddExample([ 1, 0 ], "yes")

methods.name: Emphasis
methods.description: EVERY MARK IS DERIVED, NEVER PLACED. Its geometry comes from the picture's solved values or from a rule actually in force -- which is the whole point of the plane, because a mark a person positions is a mark nobody checks. Marks are minted AFTER the solve and hold every existing unknown pinned while they place themselves, so adding one cannot move the figure it describes: frame two's figure is frame one's figure, to the last pixel. A HARO, A FOCUS OR A DIM. Emphasis changes how a shape already in the picture reads, so it mints nothing for :focus and :dim -- it rewrites the shape's own stroke -- and mints one circle for :ring.

methods.name: Measure
methods.description: A DIMENSION BETWEEN TWO THINGS, WITH ITS NUMBER. The line runs centre to centre, the number is the distance FACT -- so the figure and the caption cannot disagree -- and the number's own label is solved off the ink like any other name.

methods.name: Callout
methods.description: A SENTENCE ATTACHED TO A THING. The sentence may carry a hole, and a hole is filled from a FACT rather than typed -- which is the rule the whole plane exists to enforce. The label is solved: off the ink, off other names, on the paper, exactly as a vertex's name is, which is why a callout needed no new solver.

methods.name: Show
methods.description: A RULE'S OWN BOUNDARY, AS A SHAPE. The leash a name must stay inside is a circle nobody ever drew, because it exists only as a term in the energy; showing it is reading that term's own arguments and turning them into geometry. Only the forms whose boundary IS a shape are shown, and the rest are refused by name rather than approximated.

methods.name: Region

methods.name: StartPlanar
methods.description: A PLANAR START. The solver never leaves the basin it starts in -- DN7f measured 84 crossing terms holding 10,138 energy units at convergence that no weight could spend -- so the start is where planarity is decided. A style that draws a graph declares which objects are its vertices, which shape's centre carries them, and which constructors are its edges; the diagram then seeds those centres by Tutte's embedding rather than at random. Everything else in the picture still starts where it always did.

methods.name: StartLayout
methods.description: LAYOUTS AS STARTS (DN8b). The graph plane's own engines -- hierarchical, ring, force, mesh, sequence -- computed on the graph the substance's vertices and edges make, and overlaid as the solver's start. The planar start is one of them. StartTrying names SEVERAL: the solver takes them in order, and the first that ends lawful is the picture -- so the seed is no longer what decides whether a lattice crosses.

methods.name: SetTheme

A style writes ROLES -- :primary for the one accent, :neutral for ink, :muted for secondary ink, :background for the paper -- and the theme decides what each is. A theme is named here; the diagram resolves every role through it at draw time, and a text with no colour of its own takes the best of black and white on what it sits on, measured. methods.name: SetNameOutside
methods.description: THE OPPOSITE DECLARATION: a kind whose inside is spoken for. The renderer writes a name inside any glyph big enough to hold it, which is right until the glyph holds something else -- a Petri place holds its tokens, and "Key" written over one dot read as "K.y". Declared per kind, so a notation says it once.

methods.name: SetPeerChildren
methods.description: A PARENT'S CHILDREN ARE PEERS. The layout gives a parent's column to the child that carries the longest continuation -- right for a flow, where the graph itself says "this way onward". A fault tree's gate has inputs, not a continuation: none of them is the line onward, so the gate stands at their middle whatever hangs beneath each. Declared by the notation, read by the layout.

methods.description: NOT `Function()`: Haro accepts `function` as a synonym for `func`, so a method by that name is a C6 "Error in function name" at load time. Same family as naming a variable `oR`, which folds onto the `or` keyword. an OBJECT accessor, so it is Q-only -- a plain twin would return an object, which is exactly what the plain form must never do

methods.name: MinimizeFrom
methods.description: THE ANSWER IS A RECORD, NOT A POINT, for the same reason the hypothesis tests return one: a bare answer cannot tell you it did not converge. :status says how it stopped, :evaluations is the honest cost (an iteration that line-searched twelve times is not one unit of work), and :why says it in words.

methods.name: MaximizeFrom
methods.description: THE LARGEST value, by minimising the negative. Doing it here rather than telling you to rewrite the expression is the point: -f has the same maximiser as f has minimiser, but the VALUE comes back negated, and forgetting to flip it back is the obvious way to get this wrong.

methods.name: AddKey

methods.name: SetJwks
methods.description: load a whole JWKS document ({"keys":[ {...}, ... ]}), as fetched from the provider's jwks_uri.

methods.name: AuthorizationUrl
methods.description: step 1: send the user to the provider --------------------------- The authorization URL. state defends the redirect against CSRF; nonce binds the id-token to THIS login (replay defense); PKCE (S256) stops an intercepted authorization code from being redeemed by anyone else.

methods.name: NewPkce
methods.description: a fresh PKCE verifier (kept by the app) and its S256 challenge (sent to the provider) -> [ :verifier, :challenge ].

methods.name: VerifyIdToken
methods.description: step 2: believe (or refuse) the id-token ------------------------ Verify an id-token end to end -> [ :ok, :subject, :email, :claims, :why ]. pcExpectedNonce is the nonce this login sent ("" skips that check, which is only sound for a flow that carried no nonce).

methods.name: Why
methods.description: why the last verification was refused ("" when it passed).

methods.name: Issuer
methods.description: identity + keys

methods.name: UseRsaKey
methods.description: Sign with RS256 instead, using an RSA private key you already have. Plenty of older clients accept RS256 and nothing else, so an ES256-only issuer cannot serve them. The key stays here; only its public parts reach the JWKS.

methods.name: UseNewRsaKey
methods.description: generate one, for development

methods.name: RotateKey
methods.description: Start signing with a NEW key. The previous public key stays in the JWKS, so tokens already issued keep verifying until they expire -- rotation without an outage. A 32-byte hex seed makes it deterministic ("" = random).

methods.name: JwksJson
methods.description: what a relying party fetches from jwks_uri: the CURRENT key plus any still-valid previous ones.

methods.name: DiscoveryJson
methods.description: the discovery document served at /.well-known/openid-configuration.

methods.name: RegisterClient
methods.description: the client registry --------------------------------------------- Register an application. The secret is stored HASHED (a leak of our store must not yield working client credentials). paRedirectUris is the exact set a code may be delivered to.

methods.name: Authorize
methods.description: step 1: authorize (the user is already signed in to US) ---------- Issue an authorization code for an authenticated user. paReq: [ :clientId, :redirectUri, :state, :nonce, :codeChallenge, :scope ] -> [ :ok, :code, :redirectTo, :state, :why, :error ]

methods.name: ExchangeCode

Adding two instructions aimed at the observed failures -- "do not explain the structure", and "replace every <...> with a real value" -- took it to 0/10: a small model told not to explain explained more, and the negation was the thing it echoed. methods.name: Center
methods.description: THE NAME FORM CARRIES THE SEMANTICS, which is a Softanza law rather than a style: an ACTIVE verb -- Standardize(), Center() -- DOES the thing and returns nothing; the PASSIVE form -- Standardized(), Centered() -- returns the transformed DATA and leaves the object alone; and the Q twin does the thing and returns the object so calls chain. The first version of this class had Standardized() mutating the analysis and returning This, which got both halves wrong at once: a passive name for an active act, and a plain method returning an object where plain methods return data. CENTER each feature on its mean and leave the units alone -- covariance PCA. The features that vary most, in their own units, dominate.

methods.name: Standardize

methods.name: SetProfile
methods.description: A stzPlatformProfile DESCRIBES the solution -- its constituents (a server, a superapp, an app, ...) and their target systems. The platform OWNS one and drives its lifecycle: Build() the platform and its constituents, THEN Deploy() them -- two separate, ordered operations. (SetProfile snapshots the profile, so configure it fully first -- the aliasing doctrine.)

methods.name: Build
methods.description: BUILD the platform and its constituents. Refuses an unsound solution (LAW 3). Must precede Deploy().

methods.name: Deploy
methods.description: DEPLOY the built parts to their target systems. Refuses if the platform was not built first -- Build() and Deploy() are separate. For each part, the deploy-time LOWERING bridge turns its rehearsed (up-enable) feature ops into a real target ARTIFACT (firmware source for an MCU, a manifest otherwise) -- the flash/upload of that artifact to the device is the one remaining external step.

methods.name: DeployAs
methods.description: Governed deploy: deployment is an EFFECTFUL crossing, so an actor that cannot effect reality (an LLM) may PROPOSE it but not perform it (Phase 4).

methods.name: SetWorld
methods.description: == 1. GENERATION ======================================================== SET the world this platform envelopes -- by HARVESTING its declarations into the platform's own records, right now. It does NOT hold the world: Haro copies an object into an attribute, so a held stzApp would be a dead snapshot the moment the caller touched it (see the aliasing note in the header). Call this AFTER the world is declared. The world is ASKED through its own accessors -- a platform never reaches into another object's attributes. (A constellation ADDs many worlds; a platform SETs its one.)

methods.name: Generate
methods.description: Generate(:all) or Generate(:web / :desktop / :mobile). Writes REAL shell files (one per declared Reach) and returns the list of written paths. Raises when there is no world, no reach, or an unknown reach surface (LAW 3: refuse, never stub).

methods.name: GovernedBy
methods.description: == 2. THE CAPABILITY SEAM ============================================== Wire the (fully configured, sealed) governance regime. Declares the platform's capability risk tiers into it when undeclared. the NAME of the object that governs this platform ("" if none)

methods.name: AddCapability
methods.description: Request a capability for the attached world: oPlat.AddCapabilityQ(:camera).SetPurposes([ :scan-dish-photo ])

methods.name: Granted
methods.description: The governed decision: the WORLD is the actor, "use-<cap>" the action; permission CAN + authority SHOULD vs the risk tier.

methods.name: OpenCommonsOn
methods.description: == 3. THE COMMONS RUNTIME ============================================== Identity / sessions / messaging / stores over an OPEN stzDatabase. (The stored object shares the engine handle -- live; keep the original open while the platform runs.)

methods.name: SetKdfRounds
methods.description: Tune the KDF cost. Default 100k; lower ONLY in tests. Must be set before RegisterIdentity (a stored hash is bound to the rounds used).

methods.name: RegisterIdentity
methods.description: KDF-BACKED IDENTITY (the engine KDF closes the plaintext gap): each identity stores a per-user random SALT + a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hash of the secret over @nKdfRounds iterations -- never the secret itself.

methods.name: OpenSession
methods.description: Returns a session token, or "" (Why() explains) on refusal. The secret is verified by re-deriving with the stored salt + rounds and a CONSTANT-TIME compare (StzEngineCryptoConstEqual).

methods.name: ServeBody
methods.description: == 4. THE NETWORKED BODY =============================================== Serve the harvested world over the R7 reactor host: GET /world        -> the world (name, things, screens) as json GET /thing?name=x -> one thing's fields nPort 0 = ephemeral; the bound port via HostQ().Port().

methods.name: HostQ
methods.description: The serving host (a chainable stz object -- Q-convention). NB: an accessor returns a handle-sharing copy; use it for Port()/ServeOne.

methods.name: Bond
methods.description: Declare a norm-bearing bond: from-world may attempt an action on to-world (still subject to governance at call time).

methods.name: CallAcross
methods.description: The enforcement seam: a cross-world call goes through ONLY when (a) both worlds are active in the registry, (b) a bond declares the action, and (c) governance lets the calling world proceed. Returns TRUE/FALSE; Why() explains every refusal.

methods.name: WaitForAttributetoSettle

Returns 0 on success, negative on error (-2 not found, -3 already exited, -4 not a spawn / no handle). The kill is mutex-guarded in the engine so it can't race the loop thread reaping the process on its own exit.

methods.name: Listen
methods.description: A listener lives on the loop thread; Haro drains EVENTS: [ :accept, nConn, "" ] / [ :data, nConn, cBytes ] / [ :closed, nConn, "" ] / [] when there is none. In http mode each :data event is ONE complete framed HTTP/1.1 request (headers + Content-Length body, pipelining-safe). Raw TCP stream listener (IoT/telemetry). nPort 0 = ephemeral. Returns the server id (>0) or a negative uv error code.

methods.name: ListenHttp
methods.description: HTTP/1.1 listener: :data events carry complete requests.

methods.name: ListenStzm
methods.description: STZM message-plane listener (distribution D0): each :data event is ONE complete STZM frame (header + payload). Unpack with StzmUnpack().

methods.name: ListenStzmTls
methods.description: TLS-terminating STZM listener (D5): the same framed message plane over the same mbedTLS termination the HTTPS listener uses. A non-empty cCaPath verifies client certs; bRequireClient makes a valid one MANDATORY (mutual TLS node links).
methods.signature: ListenStzmTls(cHost, nPort, cCertPath, cKeyPath, cCaPath, bRequireClient)

methods.name: ConnectStzm
methods.description: Persistent CLIENT CHANNEL to a peer (distribution D0). The dial is async: the channel id comes back immediately; link-up arrives as an :accept event on ServerPoll/Await (a failed dial as :closed). The channel then speaks the SAME calls a listener does -- ServerWrite to send, ServerPoll to receive, ServerStop to hang up. A link is a link, whichever side dialed.

methods.name: ConnectRaw
methods.description: Raw-stream client channel (:data events carry stream chunks).

methods.name: ConnectStzmTls
methods.description: STZM channel over CLIENT-role TLS (the mTLS counterpart of ListenTls, on the persistent link): this node PRESENTS cCertPath/cKeyPath for the peer's mutual check ("" for none) and VALIDATES the peer -- see _TlsVerifyMode() for what bVerify may be. Link-up (:accept) fires only when the handshake COMPLETES -- an up channel is a SECURE channel.
methods.signature: ConnectStzmTls(cHost, nPort, cCertPath, cKeyPath, cCaPath, bVerify)

methods.name: WaitLinkUp
methods.description: Block up to nTimeoutMs for the channel's link-up. Returns the conn id (> 0) to write on, or 0 (dial failed or timed out).

methods.name: ListenHttpTls
methods.description: TLS-terminating HTTP listener: each connection runs an mbedTLS handshake (server cert cCertPath + key cKeyPath) before the plaintext HTTP framing -- so the events Haro drains are DECRYPTED requests and ServerWrite responses are encrypted transparently. A non-empty cCaPath turns on client-cert verification; bRequireClient = TRUE makes a valid client cert MANDATORY (mutual TLS). Returns the server id (>0) or a negative error (TLS setup errors are -10..-17). Engine-terminated TLS.
methods.signature: ListenHttpTls(cHost, nPort, cCertPath, cKeyPath, cCaPath, bRequireClient)

methods.name: ListenHttpsServer
methods.description: One-way server TLS convenience (no client cert): serve HTTPS with just a server cert + key.

methods.name: TlsRequest
methods.description: Send cRequest (raw HTTP bytes) to cHost:nPort over TLS and return the response bytes ("" on failure -- see TlsClientStatus). This node PRESENTS the client cert cCertPath/cKeyPath (for the peer's mutual check; pass "" for none), and VALIDATES the peer's server cert (hostname checked via SNI) -- see _TlsVerifyMode() for bVerify. A dedicated mbedTLS transport (PEM certs + mutual auth), separate from the curl path used for general outbound HTTPS.
methods.signature: TlsRequest(cHost, nPort, cRequest, cCertPath, cKeyPath, cCaPath, bVerify)

methods.name: TlsGet

methods.signature: TlsGet(cHost, nPort, cPath, cCertPath, cKeyPath, cCaPath, bVerify)

methods.name: TlsClientStatus
methods.description: Result of the last TlsRequest: 0 ok, -1 connect, -2 handshake (an untrusted/invalid peer SERVER cert aborts here), -3 cert verify, -4 setup, -18 verification switched off without :InsecureNoVerify, -19 no trust anchor. NOTE: a server rejecting a MISSING client cert is enforced SERVER-side -- under TLS 1.3 the client's handshake still completes (status 0) but the protected response comes back EMPTY. So the authoritative "was I let in?" check is the RESPONSE body, not status.

methods.name: AddCase
methods.description: A PICTURE THE RULES ARE JUDGED AGAINST. It must already be rendered: every plastic rule reads render facts, and a diagram that has not been drawn answers with empty lists -- which would read as an empty scope and convict every rule in the set of being dead. THE CASE a rule set is judged against -- a rendered picture for the graph plane, a code graph for stzCodeRule, an agent graph, an org chart. The governance never asks what kind it is; it asks the RULES what they govern in it, which is the only thing that has to be domain-specific.

methods.name: AddPicture
methods.description: A PICTURE IS SOLVED BEFORE IT IS COPIED. Haro copies an object into a list, and a copy of an unsolved picture solves itself again the first time a scope asks it anything -- so a corpus of 52 unsolved pictures paid 52 layouts at its first question, 26 seconds of the gate's governor, and the caller's own picture paid the same again when it was asked. Solved here, in the caller's hand (a parameter is a reference), the copy carries the solution and every later copy of the caller's picture does too.

methods.name: DeclarePrecedence
methods.description: A DECLARED PRECEDENCE between two rules that reach for one subject. The reason is required: a precedence without one is a coin toss that somebody will later reverse in good faith.

methods.name: CheckCases
methods.description: the rules against the pictures ----------------------------------- What the rules say about the corpus -- the ordinary half, kept here so one call answers both halves and neither can be run without the other being available.

methods.name: CheckRules
methods.description: the rules against themselves ------------------------------------- The five questions. Every finding here is about a RULE, so :where is the rule's name and the corpus is the evidence, which is the inverse of CheckPictures and the reason both exist.

methods.name: CheckAll
methods.description: both halves, and the verdict -------------------------------------- Everything: what the rules say about the pictures, and what the governor says about the rules.

methods.name: Declare
methods.description: the dependency surface ------------------------------------------- Declare a service this solution depends on, before anything is bound. This is what turns "what does this touch?" from archaeology into a query -- and it is what lets an UNBOUND dependency be a finding rather than a surprise.

methods.name: Bind
methods.description: binding ---------------------------------------------------------- Bind an implementation. The posture is asked OF THE OBJECT: anything with IsSandbox() answering true is a sandbox. Declaring itself beats guessing from a class name, and it means a third-party double can opt in.

methods.name: BindSandbox
methods.description: ...say it explicitly when the object cannot.

methods.name: BindLocal
methods.description: Bind a genuine LOCAL equivalent -- sqlite, the filesystem, a local model. Not a fake, so unlike a sandbox this may ship; see the posture note above.

methods.name: BindLive
methods.description: Bind the real thing, naming the STORE SECRET its credential lives in. The name, not the key: a registry that held credentials would be one more place they leak from.

methods.name: Unbind
methods.description: Remove the IMPLEMENTATION but keep the dependency. The service is then declared-and-unbound, which IS a finding -- your solution still needs the thing, it just has nothing to serve it. To retire the dependency itself, use Undeclare.

methods.name: Undeclare
methods.description: Retire the dependency altogether -- the solution no longer needs this service. Unbinds it too, so nothing is left half-declared.

methods.name: Service
methods.description: resolution (what the application actually calls) ------------------ The service by name. RAISES when nothing is bound -- an unbound dependency that silently returned NULL would fail later, somewhere else, as a null-call with no hint of the real cause.

methods.name: SandboxedServices
methods.description: every service still bound to a fake -- the "what is not real yet" list.

methods.name: LocalServices
methods.description: the genuinely-local ones: real, self-hosted, shippable.

methods.name: SetPhase
methods.description: the phase -------------------------------------------------------- :development / :emulated -> sandboxes are expected. :production -> they are a violation. The phase is the SAME switch stzDelivery already uses, so nothing new decides what is real.

methods.name: FindingsVia
methods.description: governance ------------------------------------------------------- [ [ :invariant, :severity, :where, :message ], ... ] -- the same shape stzSecurityPosture and the graph rules use, so one CI gate covers all three. poStore may be NULL when there is no keyring to check against. NOTE: each _Check returns its OWN list and this LOOPS to append the elements. Haro's `+` on a list appends the whole list as ONE element, so `_aF_ + This._Check...()` would nest rather than accumulate -- and a nested findings list silently reports zero errors. Same shape as stzSecurityPosture.

methods.name: MayGoLive
methods.description: ASKED IN THE PRODUCTION FRAME, whatever the current phase. "May I go LIVE?" IS the production question, so answering it from a :development phase would have said YES with a fake still bound -- the phase-dependent invariants (sandbox-in-production, ephemeral-in-production) simply had not fired yet. The phase is set, the surface judged, the phase restored: asking is not declaring. (Found while writing the narration; the guard had only ever asked after setting production, so the honest answer and the convenient one agreed.)

methods.name: FindingsForProductionVia
methods.description: the surface judged as production would judge it, then put back

methods.name: WhyNotLive
methods.description: ...and the same, but explaining itself.

methods.name: AsRuleGraph
methods.description: NOTE this does NOT duplicate the invariants above. Findings from Findings() already carry the report's shape, so the registry joins the shared CI gate directly:  oReport.IngestLegacy(oReg.Findings(), "services"). What the GRAPH adds is the question a flag check cannot ask -- which PART of a solution depends on a fake -- and that needs the delivery's parts joined to these nodes (see stzDelivery.AsRuleGraph and stzServiceRuleSet).

methods.name: MakeSilence
methods.description: lifecycle

methods.name: BufferId
methods.description: Hand the engine id out -- for a graph that wants this sound as a source. An ENGINE handle, not a pointer, so it obeys the house law.

methods.name: Frames
methods.description: readers: they return DATA and keep their names

methods.name: SampleAt
methods.description: ONE sample. 1-based frame and channel, like every Haro face.

methods.name: ToList
methods.description: The samples of one channel, as a Haro list. DATA, so To... is right. Be aware this crosses the FFI once per sample -- fine for a look at a few thousand frames, wrong for a whole song.

methods.name: ResampleTo
methods.description: verbs that change the sound ---------------------------------------- Resample to a new rate. QUALITY is sinc unless you ask otherwise -- SN1 measured sinc at 97x the accuracy of linear for 26x the cost, and still 150x faster than real time, so it is the right default.

methods.name: ToWavBytes
methods.description: The symmetric half of loading from memory, and its absence was a real gap: a sound could be decoded FROM bytes but not encoded back TO them, so handing a buffer to another tier meant a temporary file. VC1 went to some trouble to keep a voice out of the filesystem; without this, VC3 would have put it straight back to feed a recogniser.

methods.name: MixIn
methods.description: 16-bit by default: it is what everything reads, and SN1 measured the round-trip error at 4.18e-5, one quantum. Ask for 32 when you are handing the file back to another stage rather than to a listener. ADD another sound into this one from pnSeconds in, scaled by pnGain -- notes laid on a timeline. Refused when the sample rates differ: a note mixed at the wrong rate would be a different pitch, silently.

methods.name: Play
methods.description: hearing it ---------------------------------------------------------- PLAY IT, and wait for it to finish. There is no sample-player in the engine -- the device sink plays a STREAM -- so the face builds the smallest graph that can carry this sound and runs it. That is what a declarative face is for: the caller says "play", not "make a graph, start a producer thread, open a device, wait, then take it all down".

methods.name: ToSpectrum
methods.description: To...() because these RETURN things. A spectrum is a stzSoundGrid: rows by columns of numbers, with x_step and y_step saying what a row and a column MEAN. Drawing one is the graphics plane's job, and keeping that boundary is what makes the analysis assertable -- "the 1 kHz sine is in the 1 kHz bin" is a claim about numbers; "the picture looks right" is a claim about nothing. The magnitude spectrum of one window. Default 4096 points: about 12 Hz resolution at 48 kHz, which resolves musical pitch without smearing time.

methods.name: ToSpectrogram
methods.description: Frequency against time: one row per window. MULTICORE by default -- every row is an independent FFT over a different slice of the same immutable buffer, which is the one analysis here that parallelises without an argument.

methods.name: DominantFrequency
methods.description: The strongest frequency present, in hertz.

methods.name: ToOnsets
methods.description: Where notes START, in seconds -- a one-row grid of times.

methods.name: Tempo
methods.description: Beats per minute, or -1 when there are too few onsets to say -- which is a better answer than a confident number derived from two events.

methods.name: Loudness
methods.description: The standard's K-weighting coefficients are specified at 48 kHz, and the engine REFUSES any other rate rather than applying them anyway. So the face resamples a COPY when it has to -- the caller's sound is not touched, and nobody gets a plausible-looking wrong number.

methods.name: MomentaryLoudness
methods.description: MomentaryLoudness is the standard's own 400 ms window, ungated, taking the LOUDEST such window rather than a mean -- averaging an earcon against the silence around it answers nothing. BS.1770 arithmetic used as specified, so it is LUFS without qualification.

methods.name: LoudnessOfSupport
methods.description: The same K-weighting and the same formula over the sound's OWN length. NOT a standard LUFS figure, and LoudnessMetric() says so -- because the alternative is answering the standard's question wrongly instead of answering a different question honestly. A 60 ms earcon at peak 0.5 reads -9.26 here against -9.27 for the same tone at 400 ms: the two agree to a hundredth of a decibel where the standard has an opinion, which is what makes this trustworthy where it does not.

methods.name: LoudnessMetric
methods.description: What the number means, so it never travels without its method.

methods.name: Vowels
methods.description: The five vowels, and the first two formants each sits on at a pitch -- what the guard holds the rendered spectrum against.

methods.name: Vowel
methods.description: One vowel at a pitch (a note name or Hz) for `pnSeconds`.

methods.name: Sing
methods.description: SINGING -- gated by the verdict. Refused, with the reason, until the author has heard the formant voice and called it singing.

methods.name: Reshape
methods.description: Start over with a different shape. Only legal before anything is added.

methods.name: OutputNode
methods.description: Which node the graph currently hands to the world, as an index. A caller rarely needs this; a TRANSPORT does, because it has to reach behind the names and put something after whatever the output turned out to be.

methods.name: AddMasterGain
methods.description: This is what a transport fades on pause. It exists as a verb here rather than in the transport because only the graph knows what its output IS -- and putting one gain at the end means a pause is one click-free ramp instead of a walk over every voice, whatever the caller built upstream.

methods.name: NameIt
methods.description: naming -------------------------------------------------------------- Label the LAST node added, so later verbs can refer to it by name.

methods.name: NodeNamed
methods.description: Resolve a name OR a raw node number to a node index. Unknown names are an error the caller hears about, never a silent 0.

methods.name: AddOscillator
methods.description: the sources --------------------------------------------------------- WAVEFORM BY NAME, not by number: :Sine :Triangle :Square :Saw.

methods.name: AddSound
methods.description: Play an existing sound (a stzSound, or an engine buffer id) as a source.

methods.name: AddTimeline
methods.description: MU2: a node whose output is the notes placed on it, each at the frame asked -- inside a block, not at its top. It has no input. Returns the node (1-based), which StzEngineSoundGraphTimelinePlace takes.

methods.name: AddGainOn
methods.description: the shapers: each takes WHAT it acts on, by name

methods.name: AddEnvelopeOn
methods.signature: AddEnvelopeOn(pName, pnAttack, pnDecay, pnSustain, pnRelease, pnHold)

methods.name: AddEnvelopeOnAt
methods.description: The same envelope, starting nStart seconds in. THIS is what makes a score possible: a voice that knows WHEN it sounds is a note.
methods.signature: AddEnvelopeOnAt(pName, pnAttack, pnDecay, pnSustain, pnRelease, pnHold, pnStart)

methods.name: AddEchoOn
methods.description: ECHO, not "reverb". SN4's challenge pass refused to call a delay a reverb: one repeat fading out is not a diffuse room, and a name that promises a hall and delivers a slapback survives into documentation.

methods.name: AddMixOf
methods.description: mixing -------------------------------------------------------------- Mix several named nodes into one. The engine requires every input to EXIST before the mix does -- that is what makes a cycle impossible -- so this verb takes them all at once rather than letting you add to a mix later and discover the refusal.

methods.name: SetOutputTo
methods.description: output -------------------------------------------------------------- Which node the graph hands to the world. Defaults to the last thing added, which is right far more often than not.

methods.name: ToSound
methods.description: Render nSeconds and hand back a stzSound. DATA, so To... is right.

methods.name: Rewind
methods.description: Rewind every stateful node so the next render starts from the top.

methods.name: PlayFor
methods.description: hearing it

methods.name: Underruns
methods.description: How many frames the last PlayFor could not supply. Zero is the answer you want, and the plane counts it rather than letting you guess.

methods.name: Rows
methods.description: shape and meaning

methods.name: SecondsPerRow
methods.description: What one row STEP means in time, for a spectrogram. 0 when a row is not a moment (a spectrum, an onset list).

methods.name: HertzPerColumn
methods.description: What one column means in frequency. 0 when a column is not a frequency.

methods.name: PeakColumnOfRow
methods.description: Which column holds the largest value in a row -- "which frequency won".

methods.name: PeakFrequencyOfRow
methods.description: The same answer in hertz, which is what you actually wanted.

methods.name: ToList
methods.description: One row as a plain Haro list. DATA, so To... is right. It crosses the FFI once per value, so it is for looking at a row, not at a whole spectrogram -- ToCanvas does that without ever building a Haro list.

methods.name: ToTimesList
methods.description: The whole of a one-row grid -- an onset list is exactly this.

methods.name: ToCanvas
methods.description: Recorded as an SN5 finding: an AddImage on stzCanvas would turn this from thousands of rectangles into one call, and the graphics plane is where that belongs.

methods.name: ToCanvasOf
methods.description: pnMaxBins caps how much of the spectrum is drawn: nearly all musical energy lives in the bottom fraction of the range, and drawing 2048 bins up to Nyquist wastes most of the picture on silence.

methods.name: ToSVGFile
methods.description: Write the picture. SVG always works -- it needs no device at all, which is what lets a CI machine draw a spectrogram.

methods.name: ToPNG
methods.description: PNG goes through the GPU tier, so it needs a device. SVG does not.

methods.name: IsUsable
methods.description: what it is

methods.name: HonestName
methods.description: The name it ships under if the author's ear says the real one lies.

methods.name: PitchClass
methods.description: harmonic: held to 2 cents. inharmonic: a bar, a bell or a drum, whose partials are not multiples -- its lowest mode is checked, its perceived pitch is the listener's. none: a hi-hat or a snare.

methods.name: ToSoundOf
methods.description: a note, as data

methods.name: ToSoundOfGlide
methods.description: A pitch that MOVES while it sounds -- a talking drum squeezed, a bow sliding. Strings plucked and FM voices hold one pitch and refuse this.

methods.name: ToSoundOfStroke
methods.description: Where a drum is struck. Hand drums: :Dum (centre), :Tak (rim), :Ka (the weaker rim). The kit: :Kick, :Snare, :HiHat.

methods.name: RawCents
methods.description: what the last note needed

methods.name: SetTempo
methods.description: settings

methods.name: CaptureInsteadOfDevice
methods.description: WHAT IT CANNOT STAND IN FOR: a device drains on ITS OWN thread, so while this thread is busy rendering a new loop's notes the card keeps playing what was posted. Here THIS thread is the consumer, so it stalls with the render and nothing is consumed. Whether a render while playing costs a note its frame is therefore a DEVICE question, and the guard asks it on the device.

methods.name: LiveLoop
methods.description: NAMED LiveLoop, NOT Loop. The plan's section 4 writes oM.Loop(...), and that line cannot be written in Haro: `loop` is a keyword (it is Haro's `continue`), and a method may not take its name. LiveLoop is also Sonic Pi's word for the same thing (live_loop).

methods.name: LiveLoopOf
methods.description: A loop given a pattern object -- one already transformed by the algebra.

methods.name: Every
methods.description: The plan's line: every n cycles, the loop transformed. A redefinition like any other -- it lands on a boundary.

methods.name: Silence
methods.description: Stop one loop at the next boundary it can land on.

methods.name: Start
methods.description: running

methods.name: Tick
methods.description: Post what is due, drain (capture mode), and report what is heard.

methods.name: WaitCycles
methods.description: Play for `pnCycles` more cycles of HEARD time, ticking all the while.

methods.name: DriveWith
methods.description: The reactive plane drives it instead: one timer, every 20 ms, for every session registered -- see StzSoundLiveTickAll above for why it is global.

methods.name: Release
methods.description: Free the notes and the graph -- only once stopped: the timeline reads the notes' samples directly.

methods.name: IsRunning
methods.description: what happened

methods.name: HeardFrames
methods.description: Frames the listener has been given: the device's consumed frames, or what capture mode has drained.

methods.name: ConsoleLog
methods.description: [ cycle, heardFrame, text ] -- one line per cycle as it was HEARD

methods.name: Landings
methods.description: [ name, version, landingCycle, heardCycleAtCall ]

methods.name: MidCycleChanges
methods.description: Withdrawals the engine refused because the note was already sounding -- a change that would have landed MID-CYCLE. MU3's kill criterion is that this stays 0.

methods.name: ToABC
methods.description: ABC 2.1

methods.name: ToMusicXML
methods.description: MusicXML (partwise)

methods.name: ToMidiFile
methods.description: MIDI (Standard MIDI File, type 1)

methods.name: DistinctNotes
methods.description: The distinct notes and strokes over the first `pnCycles` cycles -- what a player renders BEFORE it starts: DistinctValues, in sound's word.

methods.name: IsAllStrokes
methods.description: True when every word is a stroke: the pattern names its own drum.

methods.name: ToScoreQ
methods.description: `pnCycles` cycles as a stzSoundScore, a cycle being four beats. The pivot: a pattern is a function, a score is data, and this is where one becomes the other.

methods.name: SetNote
methods.description: One line under the plot saying what the picture MEANS. A chart that needs a paragraph of explanation elsewhere is a chart that failed.

methods.name: ToNoteLines
methods.description: The note as it will actually be laid out -- DATA, so To... is right. It exists so a guard can check the wrapping without reading the picture: text reaches the SVG as glyph OUTLINES, not as characters, so there is nothing in the output to read the sentence back out of.

methods.name: DrawSpectrogram
methods.description: THE SPECTROGRAM ----------------------------------------------------- Time across, frequency up, magnitude as lightness. nMaxHz crops the top: nearly all musical energy lives low, and drawing to Nyquist spends most of the picture on silence.

methods.name: DrawSpectra
methods.description: THE SPECTRUM (one or more series) ----------------------------------- paSeries: [ [cLabel, oGrid], ... ] -- each a one-row spectrum grid. Log frequency across, decibels up. Several series is a CATEGORICAL job: fixed hue order, a legend always, and a direct label on each line.

methods.name: DrawWave
methods.description: THE WAVEFORM

methods.name: MarkTimeAt
methods.description: A vertical marker with a label -- for pointing at the moment something happens ("the click is HERE").

methods.name: MarkFrequencyAt
methods.description: The same marker on a LOG frequency axis -- for pointing at a filter's corner, a fundamental, or Nyquist. The from/to must match the DrawSpectra call, because the axis is only as wide as what was drawn on it.

methods.name: Spoken
methods.description: The syllable as SAPI says it, slowly -- the raw material, unretuned.

methods.name: Syllable
methods.description: The syllable held on a note (a name or Hz) for `pnSeconds`, at 48 kHz.

methods.name: LineQ
methods.description: Syllables on notes, a beat each, laid end to end.

methods.name: Sing
methods.description: SINGING -- gated by the retuned voice's own verdict.

methods.name: SetLookahead
methods.description: settings ------------------------------------------------------------ Frames of lookahead. Set it small only to PROVE the engine counts lateness -- the negative sibling in the guard does exactly that.

methods.name: Prepare
methods.description: the instruments' work, done first

methods.name: Play
methods.description: live, on the device

methods.name: Tick
methods.description: Post what is due, let the transport keep its clock, and stop once the last note has played out on the device.

methods.name: RenderThroughRing
methods.description: The SAME real-time path -- a producer thread rendering the graph into a ring, this thread posting notes ahead of it -- with this thread also draining the ring instead of a sound card. It runs as fast as the machine can, which is HARDER for the scheduler than a device: the producer is never waiting for the speaker. What comes out is returned as a sound, so a guard can hold it against the offline render sample for sample.

methods.name: Placed
methods.description: what happened

methods.name: Late
methods.description: Notes whose frame the producer had already rendered when they arrived.

methods.name: Underruns
methods.description: Frames the device asked for and the ring could not supply, as of the last tick -- the producer falling behind, which is a different failure from a note posted late, and counted separately.

methods.name: Release
methods.description: Free the notes. Only once nothing is playing: the timeline reads their samples directly, and a freed note under a playing timeline is a read of freed memory.

methods.name: Note
methods.description: building ------------------------------------------------------------ One pitched note, after everything already in the score. `pNote` is a note name ("A4", "C#3", "Bb2", "D4+50") or a frequency in Hz.

methods.name: GlideAt
methods.description: MU4: a note whose pitch MOVES from one pitch to another over its whole length -- a meend, a Zarma slide, a kalangu's squeezed tone. Names or Hz.

methods.name: NoteAt
methods.description: MU3: a note at an explicit beat, for a score built from a pattern. It does not move where the next Note() goes; the length grows to cover it.

methods.name: SetLength
methods.description: The length in beats, set outright -- a pattern's cycles end where they end, whatever their last note does.

methods.name: Stroke
methods.description: A struck sound on a membrane -- :dum, :tak, :ka, or :kick, :snare, :hihat on the kit. Which drum strikes it is the instrument's business (On).

methods.name: AddNotes
methods.description: Space-separated names, one beat each; the octave carries; ~ rests.

methods.name: Then
methods.description: the algebra --------------------------------------------------------- SEQUENCE: the other score starts where this one ends.

methods.name: Together
methods.description: PARALLEL: the other score starts where this one starts. The length is the longer of the two.

methods.name: Repeat
methods.description: The same score, n times in sequence.

methods.name: On
methods.description: AND it names the notes this score gains AFTERWARDS by Note and Stroke. The first cut was the pure modifier only, and the very first smoke test fell into it: StzSoundScoreQ().On(:Drumkit) then twenty strokes named NOTHING (the score was empty when On ran), so every stroke went to the default piano and was refused. A rule that the first user breaks in the first line is the rule's fault. Scores joined by Then or Together keep their own naming -- an unnamed part stays unnamed until an outer On names it.

methods.name: Transpose
methods.description: Semitones, fractional allowed (0.5 is a quarter tone). Strokes keep their pitch: a transposed drum pattern is the same drum pattern.

methods.name: SetVelocity
methods.description: The velocity of notes ADDED FROM NOW ON, 0 < v <= 1.

methods.name: Tempo
methods.description: the performance settings

methods.name: Quantize
methods.description: Snap every start to the nearest multiple of `pnGrid` beats (0.25 = a sixteenth). 0 turns it off. Durations are left alone.

methods.name: Swing
methods.description: SWING: the first of each PAIR of subdivisions lasts `pnRatio` of the pair. 0.5 is straight, 2/3 is a triplet swing, 0.75 a dotted one. Every position is warped, not only those on the grid -- the first half of each pair is stretched and the second compressed, piecewise-linearly -- so a note between two grid points moves with its neighbours instead of jumping past one.

methods.name: Events
methods.description: reading it ---------------------------------------------------------- The events in start order. A copy: changing it changes nothing here.

methods.name: PitchedEvents
methods.description: The plan's fourth transform: key, mode, density, contour -- Music21's side, on the same stzSoundScore every other transform makes and reads. the pitched events, in start order

methods.name: RangeInCents
methods.description: lowest to highest pitch, in cents

methods.name: Density
methods.description: pitched notes per beat

methods.name: Contour
methods.description: "U", "D" or "S" from each pitched note to the next -- S within 5 cents

methods.name: BestModes
methods.description: WHICH DECLARED MODE FITS: every mode of every universe, every note tried as its tonic, scored by how far (in cents) each note sits from the nearest degree of the mode, going up or coming down -- the mean. [ universe, mode, tonicHz, meanCentsOff ], best first. It ranks the DECLARATIONS; a tie is reported as a tie.

methods.name: FrameOf
methods.description: WHERE A BEAT LANDS, in 0-based frames at `pnRate`: quantised, then swung, then timed. The one place beats become frames -- the offline render and the live scheduler both call it, so they cannot disagree about when a note is.

methods.name: ToSound
methods.description: performing it ------------------------------------------------------- The whole performance, rendered offline into one sound. Every note is the instrument's (MU1), placed at FrameOf() by mixInto.

methods.name: Plan
methods.description: [ frame0, bufferId ] per event, in start order; rendered on first ask.

methods.name: BufferFor
methods.description: MU3: one note's buffer, rendered once -- the live loops ask for notes one at a time. [ start, beats, hz, instrument, velocity, stroke ]

methods.name: init
methods.description: present on purpose: "new X()" WITH parentheses calls init, and fails when there is none ("Calling Function without definition: init")

methods.name: State
methods.description: what it is doing

methods.name: Refusals
methods.description: How many moves the state machine refused. A transport that is being driven wrongly says so in a number rather than misbehaving quietly.

methods.name: PositionInFrames
methods.description: Frames the DEVICE has consumed, not frames the graph has produced: the producer runs ahead by a ring's worth, so asking it would report a position up to a third of a second in the future. What the listener has heard is what the device has taken.

methods.name: Underruns
methods.description: Frames the producer could not supply in time. Zero is the answer you want, and it is counted rather than guessed.

methods.name: Play
methods.description: the moves

methods.name: PlayFor
methods.description: Play, and stop by itself after pnSeconds. The stop happens in Tick(), so it needs someone to be ticking -- RunFor and DriveWith both do.

methods.name: Resume
methods.description: The graph carries on from where it was: pausing did not rewind it, so an envelope half way through its decay is still half way through it.

methods.name: Rewind
methods.description: Back to the top: the graph rewinds and the clock goes with it. Only legal when stopped, because rewinding under a running device is a jump.

methods.name: Tick
methods.description: being driven -------------------------------------------------------- One step. Cheap on purpose: it reads a counter and decides whether the sound has run out. Call it as often as you like.

methods.name: RunToEnd
methods.description: Tick until it stops, without a reactive loop. This DOES occupy the thread -- it is the honest version of PlayFor for a script that has nothing else to do, and it still reports the position while it runs.

methods.name: RunFor
methods.description: Same as PlayFor: Play, and stop by itself after pnSeconds. The stop happens in Tick(), so it needs someone to be ticking -- RunFor and DriveWith both do.

methods.name: DriveWith
methods.description: THE REACTIVE CONVERGENCE. The transport does not own a loop; it owns a STEP. Hand it a stzReactive and the loop that already exists calls the step, alongside every timer, stream and task that loop is already carrying -- which is the whole point of there being one loop.

methods.name: OnStarted
methods.description: what to call

methods.name: Release
methods.description: housekeeping

methods.name: Mode
methods.description: choosing

methods.name: NoCycle
methods.description: The phrase ALONE: a cycle of `pnBeats` with no layers and no accents -- to hear a mode without its rhythm, or to measure a melody note with nothing struck on top of it.

methods.name: CentsOf
methods.description: the pitch vocabulary ------------------------------------------------- Cents above the tonic of degree `pcDegree` ("5", "5_", "9"), reached going UP (pbDown FALSE) or DOWN. -1 when the mode declares no scale.

methods.name: Check
methods.description: The movement rules this mode declares, held against a phrase: a list of what breaks them, each as text. An empty list is a phrase the declaration permits -- not a phrase a musician would call right.

methods.name: PerformQ
methods.description: performing a phrase --------------------------------------------------- The phrase, once per cycle for `pnCycles` cycles, in this mode, over this cycle, with its ornaments and accents, as a stzSoundScore. One phrase cycle fills one rhythmic cycle, however many beats that has.

methods.name: Sentences
methods.description: The declared sentences of a TONAL language, drummed: the plan's MU7 row (text -> drum) needs the declaration first, and it is here. Each syllable is a stroke at the pitch its tone asks for -- High, Low, or a Falling glide from High to Low -- lasting its declared units (a long vowel takes two). The interval between High and Low is the declaration's :tonepitch, which says where it came from.

methods.name: SonifyQ
methods.description: The plan's MU7 row "data -> melody in a declared universe": sonification that a listener from the tradition would hear as music, not as a meter. The lowest value sits on degree 1 and the highest two octaves of the mode up; one note per beat of the cycle, the cycle's own rhythm under it, the mode's movement and ornaments applied as for any phrase. A series with no spread is refused rather than played as one repeated note.

methods.name: SonifiedDegrees
methods.description: the degrees the last SonifyQ chose, one per value

methods.name: SonifiedTop
methods.description: the highest degree it allowed -- 2n, or fewer when the instrument is short

methods.name: ToneSyllables
methods.description: ToneSyllables returns what was read; DrumTonesQ plays it on the drum. SayOnDrum is the verb the plan names, and it is GATED: text -> drum is speech only if a Hausa speaker hears the sentence back, and until one has (the declaration's :talkingdrum verdict), it refuses with that reason.

methods.name: PlayedNotes
methods.description: [ beat, degree, cents, hz, ornament ] for every melody note the last PerformQ placed -- what a guard, or a curious reader, holds it against.

methods.name: Start
methods.description: The clock ------------------------------------------------ Start() restarts from zero (fresh span, fresh laps, fresh wall anchor) -- the engine watch_start semantics. To continue after a Pause()/Stop() without discarding, use Resume().

methods.name: Stop
methods.description: Stop() = Pause() + stamp the span's wall end, so the record / OTel export has a closed [start, end] interval.

methods.name: ElapsedMs
methods.description: The house unit is milliseconds (see the engine time bridge).

methods.name: Lap

methods.name: Record
methods.description: The record (Softanza-native serialization)

methods.name: JoinTrace
methods.description: Adopt an incoming traceparent so this span joins an existing trace instead of opening a fresh one.

methods.name: ToOtelSpan
methods.description: OpenTelemetry export (industry interop) ------------------ The span as a hashlist in OTel vocabulary. Absolute anchors in unix NANOS as STRINGS (integer ms + "000000" -- exact, since f64 cannot hold epoch nanos); exact ns duration as an attribute.

methods.name: ToOtelJson
methods.description: One OTLP-style span as a JSON string.

methods.name: Explain
methods.description: Legibility

methods.name: Frame
methods.description: the frames ----------------------------------------------------------- Open a frame. The one before it closes here: its caption is filled from the facts bound to it, its picture is drawn and judged, and neither can be changed afterwards.

methods.name: FrameOf
methods.description: the same, on a different picture: a narration may show two solves of one content, or two contents that make one point

methods.name: ExpectFindings
methods.description: A FRAME MAY BE ABOUT A PICTURE THE GATE FINDS FAULT WITH, and that is not a defect in the telling -- it is often the point. "Here is what goes wrong" is a frame whose picture is meant to be unlawful. So a frame says so, and then the gate's findings are its SUBJECT rather than its failure. A frame that expects findings and gets none is itself reported, because a flag nobody checks is a flag that rots.

methods.name: Bind
methods.description: BIND A HOLE TO A FACT. The fact is read when the frame closes, not now, so an action later in the same frame still moves the number.

methods.name: BindFact
methods.description: A FACT FROM ANOTHER PLANE. The fact shape is one shape on purpose (DN9b), so a verdict an org chart reached, or a count a notation picture keeps, can be quoted in a caption about a drawing of it. The caller supplies the fact; the storyboard still holds the caption to it, which is the whole point of binding rather than typing.

methods.name: Show
methods.description: what a frame may do to the picture

methods.name: Act
methods.description: AN ACTION IS WHAT TURNS A PICTURE INTO A DEMONSTRATION. Between two frames something changes -- a point is dragged, a datum is set -- and the next frame shows what that did. The verbs are the picture's own.

methods.name: NumberOfFrames
methods.description: what the storyboard is, once written

methods.name: NumberOfHoles
methods.description: how many numbers this narration shows, all of them from facts

methods.name: Judge
methods.description: EVERY FRAME THROUGH THE GATE, EVERY HOLE HELD TO ITS FACT. The second half is what makes a filled caption evidence rather than decoration: the number the reader sees must be the number the fact reported, and a hole the author never bound must not survive into the sentence.

methods.name: Render
methods.description: the folio, and the page --------------------------------------------- The frames are already drawn, one file each, as they closed. This writes the page that puts them in order with their sentences.

methods.name: ToNarration
methods.description: The question of whether this shape conforms was routed to the sibling through Central as DN9-EMITTER-01 and is unanswered; silence is not a veto here, so this is written, pinned and marked, and a correction costs one function.

methods.name: Rendition
methods.description: A VALUE THAT SAYS WHAT IT IS (DN9g) --------------------------------- A STORYBOARD IS NOT A PICTURE, and its rendition says so by its kind: markup, the page that puts its frames in order. A consumer choosing a surface from the kind alone therefore opens it as a document rather than trying to draw it, without knowing what class it came from.

methods.name: Fact
methods.description: reading the picture, without being able to mutate it by accident

methods.name: operator
methods.description: Haro's `obj[n]` syntax dispatches to operator("[]", n). For stzString we want the n-th codepoint (1-based). Negative n counts from the end: Q("ABCDE")[-1] = "E", [-2] = "D".

methods.name: InfereType
methods.description: Infer the canonical Softanza type named by this string. Used by the global InfereType(cType). Scalars collapse to :Number/:String/:Char (Stz-prefixed to :StzNumber/...); non-stz list/pair types collapse to the generic :List; stz-prefixed list types keep their (de-pluralised) canonical name (e.g. StzListsOfNumbers -> :StzListOfNumbers). Delegates to a file-scope helper: inside this class StartsWith / StzFind / StzReplaceCS resolve to stzString METHODS (wrong arity -> R20); at file scope they resolve to the global funcs.

methods.name: DiacriticsRemoved
methods.description: Dotless / DotsRemoved: return the content with dots stripped from "i" and "j" (Unicode "Latin Letter Dotless I" / "Dotless J"). Lossy on purpose -- meant for the typographic effect, not for round-trippable encoding. Port from archive line 93405. DiacriticsRemoved: strip combining diacritic codepoints from the content. Uses NFD normalisation to decompose accented letters into base + combining marks, then drops any codepoint in the combining ranges: U+0300-U+036F   Combining Diacritical Marks (Latin etc.) U+0610-U+061A   Arabic U+064B-U+065F   Arabic Tashkil (Fatha, Damma, ...) U+06D6-U+06ED   Arabic supplementals U+0951-U+0954   Vedic / Devanagari

example.code:
# a French sentence loses its accents
? StzStringQ("C'était un énoncé accentuée, à vrai-dire, extrâ!").DiacriticsRemoved()
# an Arabic greeting loses its harakat
? StzStringQ("السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ").DiacriticsRemoved()
example.output:
C'etait un enonce accentuee, a vrai-dire, extra!
السلام عليكم
